slides.text:
Slices and maps already hide pointers inside them. This module shows where that sharing helps and where it surprises you.

You will pass slices to functions, keep structs and pointers in slices and maps, and copy data so two values stop sharing.

A slice is a small header: a pointer to an array, a length and a capacity. Passing a slice copies the header, not the elements.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
slice header
    points to: array
    length: 3
    capacity: 3
function gets a copy of the header

slides.text:
Both headers point at the same elements, so a write by index is seen by the caller. But the length lives in the header, so a longer or shorter slice stays in the function unless you take a pointer to the slice.

With a `*[]T` the function can append, shrink or cut an element out, and the caller sees it.

slides.text:
A slice of structs holds the structs themselves, one after another. A slice of pointers holds addresses that lead to structs stored elsewhere.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
[]Task    -> the tasks are inside
[]*Task   -> addresses of tasks
range gives a copy of each element

slides.text: A copy of a struct edits nothing, but a copy of a pointer still reaches the same struct. A pointer into a slice is only good while the slice keeps its array: when `append` moves it, the pointer stays behind.

slides.text:
A map value is not an address you can take, so the struct you read is a copy. Go will not even let you write `inv[key].stock--` when the values are structs.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
item = copy of map[key]
change item
map[key] = item

slides.text: A map of pointers avoids the copy: the pointer is the value, and you change the struct it points at. A key that is missing gives a nil pointer, so check before you use it.

exercises.title: A struct from a map
exercises.guide: Change a struct stored by value in a map.

chunks.guide: An item with a stock and a price.
A map gives back a copy of the struct. Change the copy, then store it back under the key.

notes.text: A copy of the stored struct.
Writes the changed copy back.

chunks.text:
inv := map[string]Item{"pen": {stock: 10, price: 2}}
    item := inv["pen"]
    item.stock--
    fmt.Println(inv["pen"].stock)
    inv["pen"] = item
    fmt.Println(inv["pen"].stock)

slides.text:
Copying a value copies what is inside it: a slice header, a map reference or a pointer. The data behind them is still the same, so both copies change it together.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
b = copy of a
b.list -> same array as a.list
b.ptr  -> same struct as a.ptr

slides.text: To get a truly separate value, build new storage and copy into it: a new slice for the elements, and a new struct for every pointer.

exercises.title: Copy a struct
exercises.guide: Pick what main prints.
exercises.explanation: `b := a` copies the struct, but the `members` field is a slice header that points at the same array, so both teams share the elements.
